The early life history of Mercenaria mercenaria begins with the fertilised egg, which at a water temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C] hatches into a D-shaped veliger larva after approximately 18 hours, corresponding to an age at birth of 0.75 days [ab = 0.75 days]. These newly emerged D-larvae possess a prodissoconch shell measuring just 0.008 cm [Lb = 0.008 cm] in diameter, a dimension that reflects the modest maternal investment per offspring. The initial wet weight of these newly hatched larvae is extraordinarily low, recorded at 0.000000022 grams [Wwb = 0.000000022 grams], a value consistent with the minute size of the egg from which they derive. Following this brief pelagic phase, the larvae progress through a trochophore stage and into a planktotrophic feeding period, during which they actively ingest phytoplankton and begin to accumulate somatic tissue. This early developmental sequence, occurring entirely within the water column, sets the stage for the ontogenetic transitions that characterise the species' complex life cycle.

As the veliger larvae of Mercenaria mercenaria continue their planktonic existence, they undergo a pronounced increase in size, reaching a diameter of 0.025 cm  by the time they become pediveligers, the stage at which they develop a functional foot and begin exploring substrates for settlement. At this point, the dry weight at metamorphosis has been estimated at 0.0000075 grams , a threshold that signals the larva's readiness for the radical transformation to benthic life. Field observations indicate that the age at metamorphosis, from the moment of hatching to the onset of settlement behaviour, is 15 days  when reared at a consistent temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C]. During this period, the larva undergoes an allometric shift that involves the loss of the velum and the development of gill structures, marking the completion of the larval-juvenile transition. This metamorphic event represents a critical bottleneck in recruitment, as successful attachment to a suitable substratum is essential for subsequent survival and growth.

Following successful settlement and metamorphosis, the post-metamorphic juvenile Mercenaria mercenaria, commonly referred to as spat, enters a prolonged phase of somatic growth that continues until the onset of reproductive maturity. The shell length at puberty, defined as the point at which individuals are capable of initiating gametogenesis, has been measured at 3 cm [Lp = 3 cm], a size that can be attained within a variable timeframe depending on local environmental conditions. Concurrently, the dry weight at puberty is approximately 0.25 grams , a value derived from the allometric relationship between shell length and tissue mass. Under optimal conditions maintained at 15 °C [T = 15 °C], the first spawning event has been documented at 1,095 days after hatching [tR = 1,095 days after hatching], marking the onset of functional reproductive activity. This protracted juvenile period reflects the substantial energetic investment required to reach a body size capable of supporting the high fecundity that characterises the adult stage.

Upon attaining reproductive maturity, the adult Mercenaria mercenaria exhibits a remarkable capacity for gamete production. This exceptionally high fecundity, calculated from a clutch size of roughly 39.5 million eggs per spawning season [Ri = roughly 39.5 million eggs per spawning season] and a single annual spawning event [F_R_i = single annual spawning event], is among the highest recorded for temperate bivalves and is an adaptive response to the high mortality rates experienced during the planktonic larval phase. The ultimate shell length of 11 cm [Li = 11 cm] represents the maximum size attained by the oldest and largest individuals in a population, a dimension that is rarely reached but serves as a benchmark for growth potential. Correspondingly, the ultimate dry weight of the somatic and reproductive tissues in such a fully grown adult has been recorded at 12.3 grams , providing a measure of the total organic mass that can be accumulated over a lifetime of filter feeding, all occurring under sustained thermal conditions of 15 °C [T = 15 °C].

The maximum lifespan of Mercenaria mercenaria has been well documented through analyses of annual growth lines in the shell; the oldest recorded individuals have reached an age of 100 years [am = 100 years] under stable environmental conditions at 15 °C [T = 15 °C]. This extraordinary longevity, exceeding a century in some populations, places the hard clam among the longest-lived of the shallow-water bivalves in the family Veneridae and is thought to be linked to its relatively low metabolic rate and high investment in structural defences. Compared to other venerids, such as the quahog Arctica islandica which can exceed 400 years, the 100-year lifespan of Mercenaria mercenaria is still remarkable and reflects a classic slow life-history strategy: late maturation, exceptionally high reproductive output, and extended adult survival. The combination of a microscopic larval stage and centenarian adulthood exemplifies the evolutionary trade-offs between early life mortality and investment in durable tissues.
